planting.note: Set small divisions or plugs in spring into gritty, sharply drained soil, spacing them to knit together over one to two seasons.

directions: This New Zealand native forms an extremely dense, hummocky mat of tiny overlapping scale-like leaves that reads from a distance as moss or fine turf rather than a flowering plant. It spreads slowly by rooting stems and is best used as a rock garden filler, stepping-stone joint planting, or small-scale lawn substitute where foot traffic is light. Give it gritty, well-drained soil and consistent moisture while it establishes; it resents waterlogged winter soil far more than it minds light shade. Trim back any flowering stems if a perfectly smooth cushion effect is wanted.

planting.note: Divide and plant rooted sections in spring into humus-rich, evenly moist soil, spacing plugs to fill in within a season or two.

directions: This New Zealand groundcover produces finely dissected, fern-like leaflets along creeping stems that root as they spread, forming a soft, low carpet useful between stepping stones or at the front of a shaded border. Its texture is markedly lacier than the more common Leptinella squalida, giving it a more delicate, feathery look in woodland and path-edge plantings. It tolerates light foot traffic once established but prefers consistent moisture and does poorly in prolonged drought or dense shade with root competition from trees. Shear lightly after its inconspicuous button flowers fade if a tidier mat is desired.
sources: Great Plant Picks (Elisabeth C. Miller Botanical Garden)

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted stem sections in spring directly over rocks or humus-rich soil in a shaded, humid site, keeping them consistently moist until new growth appears.

directions: Native to rocky woodland in East Asia, this spikemoss creeps over stones and leaf litter with wiry, scaly stems that curl inward in dry conditions and relax flat again once moisture returns. It is often used draped over boulders or logs in shaded rock gardens and moss-garden plantings, where its texture reads as a coarser, more sculptural counterpart to true mosses. Steady humidity and dappled or full shade are essential; it scorches quickly in direct sun or dry wind. Established patches can be lifted and divided to start new colonies elsewhere in the garden.

planting.note: Press small rooted pieces into damp, shaded crevices or humus-rich soil in spring, firming gently since the roots are shallow and fine.

directions: This diminutive Mediterranean-island native forms an almost moss-like sheet of tiny rounded leaves that clings tightly to damp stone, shaded walls, and the cool side of rock gardens. It is studded with minute white flowers in late spring but is grown mainly for its carpeting foliage rather than bloom. Unlike most sandworts, which prefer sun, this species wants permanently cool, moist, shaded conditions and will scorch or dry out in exposed sites. It is well suited to shaded stone paths, trough gardens, and the base of north-facing walls where few other plants form so fine a texture.

planting.note: Plant rooted sections in spring into consistently moist, humus-rich soil in a shaded, sheltered spot, since the creeping stems root readily where they touch damp ground.

directions: A low, creeping relative of the figworts, this plant produces small rounded, scalloped leaves on thread-fine stems that root at every node, quickly knitting into a soft green mat in cool, damp, shady corners. It is native to wet banks and streamsides in western Europe and performs best where soil stays reliably moist, such as alongside a shaded pond edge or in a woodland path joint. Growth is shallow-rooted and easily damaged by drought or foot traffic, so it suits décor niches rather than lawns. Pinch or trim stray runners to keep it within bounds, as it spreads readily in favorable conditions.
